METHODOLOGY REVIEW (round 3).

Review this proposed CANDIDATE-GENERATOR design (the 'explore' half of a daily AI-response optimization loop; the 'measure' half — a locked 3-layer eval — scores candidates):

IRIS optimization loop — CANDIDATE-GENERATOR v1 (explore half), CONSOLIDATED r3 (all round-1 + round-2 fixes folded; operational constants marked [tunable] = build/calibration params, not design-locked). Measure half = locked eval DL-0022. Top-5 cap = DL-0020. Portable loop = DL-0021.

PURPOSE: given a run's eval signal, propose candidate CHANGES to the agent stack, score them, rank them, emit top-5 for human-approved routing.

A. CANDIDATE TYPES + blast-radius tier: (1) prompt/system-instruction edits — HIGH if global prefix (all lanes), MEDIUM if lane-scoped suffix; (2) reflections/habits(notes) — HIGH global / MEDIUM domain / LOW table|user; every Type-2 candidate MUST carry {scope, scope_key} in its diff; 'landed' = merged+approved; (3) tool schema/description — MEDIUM; (4) retrieval-corpus content — EVAL-INVISIBLE (eval injects context directly, retrieval bypassed) → routed to human-judgment queue, NOT suite-scored; (5) routing/classifier code — HIGH, needs a code PR. EXCLUDED: eval fixtures + judge prompts (meta firewall) → fixture-audit queue.

B. INPUT UNIT = FAILURE CLUSTER by (L2a failure-tag + domain + lane co-filter) + low L2b cases (flagged as advisory-driven). L3 EXCLUDED from clustering until κ≥0.7. Cluster input: transcripts, executed rows, failure tags, baseline diffs, per-case L1 pass/fail. Fallback clustering axis = query-pattern-tag when a tag+domain cluster is < N.

C. MIN CLUSTER SIZE: train/holdout split activates only at N≥4 (≥2 train / ≥2 holdout), random 50/50 with logged seed. Below N=4 → candidate tagged CANNOT-VALIDATE, human-judgment only, never auto-emitted as validated.

D. GENERATION: per cluster the LLM proposes K≤3 candidates, each = {falsifiable hypothesis, change diff, target-case set, change-type, blast-radius tier, scope/scope_key for Type-2}. CROSS-CLUSTER DEDUP before ranking: candidates with near-identical (type+diff) [cosine >0.9 tunable] merge into one, union their target sets, scored once.

E. ANTI-OVERFIT / REWARD-HACKING GUARD: within each failure class split failing cases TRAIN (generator sees) / HOLDOUT (blind); a candidate counts only if it moves HOLDOUT cases of the same class to pass. HOLDOUT QUARANTINE: a case held out in run N cannot re-enter train for [N+7 tunable] runs. EXPLICIT RESIDUAL: on a ~25-pair corpus holdout is weak → the human approval gate is the PRIMARY defense; the split is a secondary signal, not a guarantee.

F. SCORING / RANKING: score each candidate PAIRWISE vs baseline across the WHOLE suite. SEVERITY: L1=3, L2a=2, L2b=1; L3 EXCLUDED from net until calibrated. net = Σ(moved-to-pass × severity) − Σ(regressions × severity). σ(JUDGE NOISE): L1 σ=0 (deterministic); L2a/L2b σ estimated by scoring 5 held-aside responses twice at temp=0 and taking SD of per-case score deltas; Var(net)=9·Var(L1)+4·Var(L2a)+1·Var(L2b); re-estimate each baseline refresh. SIGNIFICANCE: a candidate's net win must exceed 2σ(net) to count. MULTIPLE-COMPARISONS: apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q=0.05) across all holdout-passing candidates BEFORE ranking. EMISSION MINIMUMS: net>0 required for ALL tiers; additionally HIGH needs net≥2, MEDIUM ≥1. TIEBREAK: smallest blast-radius tier. EARLY-EXIT: fail holdout → skip whole-suite scoring (holdout stage precedes FDR/whole-suite stage; no conflict). SUITE-VERSION LOCK: reject cross-version scores. PER-RUN COST BUDGET [~2000 judge calls or $30, tunable]: on exhaustion emit current top-5 and flag remaining clusters 'budget-exceeded'.

G. REGRESSION GATE: disqualify (regardless of target wins) any candidate that (a) regresses an L1 or L2a gate on a previously-passing case, or (b) drops L2b below the P10 baseline floor. L3 degradation is SURFACED as a reviewer flag, not a disqualifier. For HIGH/prefix (Type-1) candidates the report card MUST include a CROSS-LANE RISK NOTE: the edit fires across all lanes but the suite only covers WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS — other lanes are unmeasured.

H. FIXTURE-GAP PATH: if a failure is judged to be a bad/ambiguous fixture rather than the agent, emit a FIXTURE-GAP NOTE {fixture_id, failure_tag, transcript evidence agent was correct, missing/ambiguous property, proposed fixture change, confidence} → P0 fixture-audit queue, NOT counted against top-5. Generator instructed to prefer a fixture-gap note over a weak-evidence prompt candidate; low-confidence notes are surfaced as a count only.

I. EMISSION: top-5 by net → morning ranked report → human approval → route to issue/PR/reflection. CONFOUNDER CARD per candidate: cluster N, holdout N, judge temp, pinned model version, baseline freshness, changes-since-baseline, FDR q-value, blast tier, cross-lane note, any risk flags.

J. BASELINE / DRIFT: refresh on (model version bump) OR ([5 tunable] approved candidates landed), whichever first — re-run suite, reset P10 floor + change counter + re-estimate σ. CUMULATIVE DRIFT GUARD: > [5 tunable] approved prompt edits since refresh triggers a re-capture proposal. DELTA-VS-LAST-BASELINE: at each refresh, compare per-case pass vs the prior baseline; any newly-regressed case raises a blocking CUMULATIVE-REGRESSION flag. EVAL-CONFIG PREREQS for any scoring: PINNED model version (not an alias), judge temp=0, baseline non-null.

K. LOOP HEALTH: (1) SENTINEL — one human-authored, previously-validated candidate is re-scored every run; if its net falls below its established value, raise LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE and halt emission that run. (2) GENERATOR MODEL != JUDGE MODEL (reduce shared-blindspot reward hacking). (3) reviewer checklist item: 'is this candidate rewarded for fluency rather than grounding?'

WORKED EXAMPLE: 4 cases tagged L2a:attribution, engagement domain, all WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS lane, all L1-PASS (findings-layer problem). N=4 → 2 train / 2 holdout (seed logged). Generator (train-only) proposes ≤3 candidates; top hypothesis 'findings drop the segment filter from prose' → Type-2 note {scope: DOMAIN, scope_key: engagement, content: 'when a query filters by segment, name the segment on every reported number'}, MEDIUM tier. Scored pairwise across the suite: must fix ≥1 holdout attribution case, clear 2σ and B-H FDR, not drop L2b below P10, regress no L1/L2a gate, and net≥1 (MEDIUM). If top-5, emitted with its confounder card + reviewer checklist for approval.

Prior-round critique to check is addressed:
Round-2 blocking fixes to CONFIRM landed with no new blocker: (1) multiple-comparisons -> Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q=0.05 across holdout-passing candidates before ranking; (2) σ(judge noise) operationalized (score 5 held-aside responses twice temp=0, SD of diffs, propagate variance, re-estimate each refresh); (3) L2b-driven candidates flagged + retrieval-corpus edits are EVAL-INVISIBLE -> human route not suite-scored; (4) net>0 required all tiers; (5) pinned model version hard gate (not alias); (6) generator model != judge model; (7) sentinel loop-health candidate; (8) cross-lane risk note on prefix/HIGH candidates (suite covers only WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS lane); (9) lane co-filter in clustering + NoteScope scope_key on Type-2; (10) cross-cluster dedup; quarantine extended. Residual acknowledged: 25-pair corpus makes holdout weak -> human gate is primary defense.

Judge ONLY through an ML/experiment-methodology lens: (1) Is the generate -> score-pairwise-vs-baseline -> rank -> emit-top-5 loop sound and does it actually produce improvement signal, not noise? (2) Is the train/holdout split of failing cases a REAL anti-overfitting guard, or is it leaky (same author, same domain, tiny N, class imbalance)? Is it applied correctly? (3) Is the ranking metric (net = target-wins*severity - regressions - cost) well-formed and non-gameable? Does it double-count or ignore variance/significance? (4) Is failure-cluster the right generation unit vs per-case? (5) Attribution: can we actually claim a candidate caused the delta? For EACH design element output AGREE or OBJECT with a concrete fix. Cite experiment-design principles (holdout hygiene, multiple-comparisons, effect size vs p-hacking).

Now I have full ground-truth context (DL-0020/0021/0022, the iris-eval audit, the locked 3-layer eval). Proceeding with the round-3 methodology review.

---

## Critique

**Summary:** The design is substantially improved from prior rounds and the round-2 fixes are confirmed landed. However, **three blocking statistical errors remain**: the BH+2σ dual-filter is methodologically malformed, the normality assumption on the net statistic is violated at N=25, and the variance propagation formula ignores within-session cross-case judge correlation. Five significant/advisory gaps also follow. The plan should not proceed to implementation until the BH application is resolved; the rest can be fixed in parallel.

---

### Round-2 fix confirmation

All 11 round-2 fixes are confirmed present in sections A–K. No round-2 blocker regressed.

---

### Element-by-element verdicts

**A. Candidate types + blast-radius tier — OBJECT (one gap)**

The CROSS-LANE RISK NOTE is required for "HIGH/prefix (Type-1) candidates" only (section G). But HIGH/global Type-2 candidates (global reflections) also fire across every domain and lane of the agent. A global note like "always name the segment on every reported number" is as cross-lane as a prefix edit, and the suite only covers WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS. The risk note obligation is absent for this case.

*Fix:* In section G, change "For HIGH/prefix (Type-1) candidates" → "For all HIGH-tier candidates (Type-1 global prefix **and** Type-2 global scope)."

---

**B. Input unit (failure cluster) — OBJECT (one unspecified constant)**

Co-filter by `(L2a failure-tag + domain + lane)` with L2b as advisory and L3 excluded until κ≥0.7 is correct and aligns with DL-0022. The fallback clustering axis is sound. **But** section B says "fallback clustering axis = query-pattern-tag when a tag+domain cluster is < N" and N is never defined. This is a different N than the min-cluster-size N=4 in section C. An implementer will invent it.

*Fix:* Add `[fallback-cluster-N tunable, seed: 3]` alongside the other tunable constants.

---

**C. Min cluster size — AGREE with advisory**

N≥4 / 50/50 / CANNOT-VALIDATE tagging is correct. The design correctly acknowledges the residual ("holdout is weak"). **Advisory only:** At N=4, holdout N=2. For a cluster consisting entirely of failing cases, if the LLM has ~10% natural variability near the pass/fail boundary, P(≥1 of 2 holdout cases flip to pass by chance) ≈ 19%. The confounder card already includes holdout N, but the human reviewer may not realize what that N implies about false-pass probability.

*Recommendation (not blocking):* Add to the confounder card a literal note: "Holdout N=2 → ~15–20% false-pass rate from judge variability alone. Human judgment is the primary defense." This is honest to the acknowledged residual.

Odd-N rounding (N=5 → 2 train/3 holdout or vice versa) is unspecified but low-stakes; default to ceiling for holdout is fine. Mark it.

---

**D. Generation — OBJECT (one operationalization gap)**

K≤3 and cross-cluster dedup before ranking are both sound. **But** section D specifies dedup by "cosine >0.9 [tunable]" on "(type+diff)" without naming the embedding model. For prose diffs ("add a sentence about segments") vs code diffs (a schema field rename), two very different models produce very different similarity spaces. A general-purpose embedding might merge "always name the segment" and "always name the time window" (both surface-similar) when they target distinct failure modes, causing genuine candidates to be incorrectly merged.

*Fix:* Specify embedding surface: embed `"{type}|{scope}|{scope_key}|{first 400 chars of diff}"` using the same model family as the generator (consistency). Add: "if type differs (e.g. Type-1 vs Type-2), skip cosine check — never merge across types regardless of diff similarity."

---

**E. Anti-overfit / reward-hacking guard — OBJECT (two issues)**

**E1 — Quarantine/baseline-refresh interaction is undefined (blocking for correctness):** Section E: a case held out in run N cannot re-enter train for `[N+7]` runs. Section J: baseline refreshes on model bump OR 5 approved candidates landed. If refresh occurs at run N+3, a case quarantined at N-1 still has 5 runs left on its clock. After the refresh the baseline resets, but the quarantine doesn't. Result: a case that influenced pre-refresh generator outputs can enter training immediately post-refresh, leaking information across the refresh boundary.

*Fix:* Add to section E: "Baseline refresh resets all quarantine clocks. Cases held out in the run immediately preceding the refresh are re-quarantined for `[N+7]` runs from the refresh date."

**E2 — Same-fixture-author structural leak not addressed:** All 25 golden pairs were authored by the same human curator with consistent phrasing and coverage choices. The train/holdout split is random within this single-author corpus. A prompt edit that overfits to the curator's writing style (e.g. echoing their preferred terminology) can pass both train and holdout without generalizing to real queries. The acknowledged residual ("holdout is weak → human gate is primary defense") is correct but understates this specific path.

*Fix (advisory):* Add to section E's EXPLICIT RESIDUAL: "additional structural leak: all 25 fixtures share a single author; an edit that exploits curator style rather than the failure mechanism passes train and holdout while failing real queries. The reviewer checklist item ('fluency vs grounding?') is the primary guard for this path."

---

**F. Scoring / ranking — OBJECT (three blocking statistical issues)**

**F1 — BH after 2σ pre-filter is methodologically malformed (blocking):**

Applying Benjamini-Hochberg *after* a 2σ pre-filter is not how multiple-comparisons correction works. BH must be applied to the **full** set of M candidate hypotheses simultaneously. The 2σ pre-filter rejects H₀ for any candidate with z<2 — it has already performed M individual tests at α≈0.023. Applying BH to the surviving subset inflates the effective FDR because the denominator (total hypotheses tested) is artificially small: BH controls FDR at `(k/m)×q` where m is the full hypothesis count, but you've replaced m with m'<m. Counterintuitively, this also isn't uniformly conservative — it can accept candidates that BH on the full set would have rejected if those candidates happen to land in a high rank among survivors.

*Fix:* Choose exactly one of:
- **(a) Permutation BH only (recommended):** For each candidate, compute a permutation p-value (reshuffle which cases the candidate improves vs baseline, compute net, repeat 1000×, p = fraction ≥ observed net). Apply BH at q=0.05 across ALL M candidates. Drop the 2σ pre-filter — BH subsumes it.
- **(b) 2σ threshold only:** Keep the 2σ threshold as the sole filter. Drop BH — it is redundant if σ is well-estimated; the per-test α≈0.023 already controls per-comparison error, and at M≤30 candidates the Bonferroni correction would be 0.023/30≈0.001, which is more conservative than BH anyway. Explicitly acknowledge this as the design choice.

Do not use both in series.

**F2 — 2σ assumes normality; net is discrete and non-normal at N=25 (blocking):**

`net = Σ(moved-to-pass × severity) − Σ(regressions × severity)` is a weighted sum of at most 25 binary outcomes with weights ∈ {1,2,3}. This is a discrete distribution. The CLT does not apply at N=25 with a handful of active cases per cluster. In practice, net takes values like {-6, -5, …, 0, …, +9} with probabilities concentrated near zero. The 2σ threshold assumes net/(σ(net)) ~ N(0,1) under H₀, which is incorrect for small discrete sums — it will over-reject (too permissive) in the tails and under-reject near center.

*Fix:* Either switch to permutation p-values (which makes F1 and F2 the same fix), or explicitly add: "The 2σ threshold is a heuristic approximation; for any candidate where net ≤ 3 (i.e., a single L1 win), the normal approximation is unreliable — flag for human review regardless of σ calculation."

**F3 — Var(net) formula assumes across-case independence; within-session judge correlation is real (significant):**

`Var(net) = 9·Var(L1) + 4·Var(L2a) + 1·Var(L2b)` assumes zero covariance across the 25 cases. In practice, a single LLM judge scoring all 25 pairs in one session exhibits within-session correlation: anchoring on early judgments, position bias, and session-level "mood" effects (Zheng et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024). If within-session covariance is positive — scores trend high or low together — the true Var(net) exceeds the formula's estimate, making the 2σ threshold *too permissive* (candidates clear it more easily than they should).

The 5-held-aside-twice procedure (at temp=0) measures *within-case* variance (does the same response score differently on re-runs?) but not *across-case* covariance (do all responses in a session trend together?).

*Fix:* Add a cross-case covariance probe to the σ re-estimation procedure: score the same 5 held-aside responses in two orderings (forward and reverse); if the mean net changes by more than 0.5 severity-weighted points between orderings, apply a 1.5× multiplier to σ(net) for that run to conservatively account for the ordering effect. Alternatively, if using permutation p-values (the F1 fix), this concern is subsumed — permutations are computed from the fixed scoring order, so any order effect is captured in the empirical null.

---

**G. Regression gate — OBJECT**

See A above — HIGH/global Type-2 candidates are missing the mandatory CROSS-LANE RISK NOTE. Otherwise sound. The L3 degradation as "flag, not disqualifier" is correct per DL-0022 (L3 is advisory until κ≥0.7).

---

**H. Fixture-gap path — AGREE with advisory**

The path is sound. "Low-confidence notes are surfaced as a count only" — the confidence threshold is unspecified (what makes a fixture-gap note low vs. high confidence?). This is not blocking but will cause inconsistent behavior.

*Advisory fix:* Define: "low-confidence = generator's stated confidence < 0.6 OR transcript evidence supports two or more alternative explanations (agent error vs. fixture gap with similar plausibility)."

---

**I. Emission — OBJECT (one gap)**

The confounder card is well-designed. **Gap:** CANNOT-VALIDATE candidates (N<4 clusters) are "never auto-emitted as validated" and routed to human-judgment only. But do they count against the top-5 cap? If 4 CANNOT-VALIDATE candidates exist and the top-5 is filled with them, zero validated candidates appear in the morning report. If they don't count against the cap, validated candidates and human-judgment candidates share the same report without a clear budget relationship.

*Fix:* Specify: "CANNOT-VALIDATE candidates appear in a separate section of the report, below the top-5 validated ranking. They do not count against the 5-slot cap. A separate human-judgment queue section lists them in cluster order, with the CANNOT-VALIDATE flag prominently marked."

---

**J. Baseline / drift — AGREE with advisory**

The refresh trigger, cumulative drift guard, and delta-vs-last-baseline comparison are all sound. **Advisory:** When the CUMULATIVE-REGRESSION flag fires (newly-failing cases at refresh), the spec cannot attribute regression to a specific landed candidate — only to the set of ≤5 candidates that landed since the prior refresh. This is acceptable for v1 but should be noted in the confounder card as a known limitation ("regression attribution granularity: batch, not per-candidate").

---

**K. Loop health — OBJECT (sentinel undefined after refresh)**

The sentinel concept is correct and the generator≠judge model constraint is good. **Bug:** Section K says "if its net falls below its established value, raise LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE." After a baseline refresh, the sentinel's net legitimately changes — if the baseline improves (some target cases now pass), the sentinel's net contribution drops to zero. Flagging this as LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE is a false alarm. Conversely, auto-updating the established value after every refresh removes the anchoring function entirely.

*Fix:* "After each baseline refresh, re-score the sentinel and update its expected net to the new score. LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE triggers only if the sentinel's net in run N is **below its net at the immediately prior run** (delta < 0 run-over-run), not vs the original establishment value. Record the full time-series of sentinel net scores for trend analysis."

---

### Recommended corrections by priority

| Priority | Issue | Section | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 🔴 Blocking | BH after 2σ pre-filter is malformed | F | Choose one: permutation BH on all M candidates, OR 2σ threshold alone. Not both. |
| 🔴 Blocking | 2σ assumes normality; net is discrete at N=25 | F | Permutation null (same fix as above) OR document the heuristic clearly and add a net≤3 human-review flag. |
| 🔴 Blocking | Var(net) ignores cross-case correlation | F | Add ordering-probe to σ estimation + 1.5× multiplier if ordering effect detected; or subsumed by permutation fix. |
| 🟡 Significant | HIGH/global Type-2 missing CROSS-LANE RISK NOTE | A, G | Extend the note requirement to all HIGH-tier candidates. |
| 🟡 Significant | Quarantine clock undefined across baseline refresh | E | Refresh resets clocks; re-quarantine prior run's holdout set. |
| 🟡 Significant | Sentinel expected value logic breaks after refresh | K | Delta-from-prior-run trigger, not delta-from-establishment-value. |
| 🟡 Significant | CANNOT-VALIDATE candidates vs top-5 cap | I | Separate section, not competing for the 5-slot cap. |
| 🟠 Advisory | Fallback cluster threshold N unspecified | B | Add `[fallback-cluster-N tunable, seed: 3]`. |
| 🟠 Advisory | Cosine dedup embedding model unspecified | D | Specify model + surface; block cross-type merges regardless of similarity. |
| 🟠 Advisory | Fixture-gap confidence threshold unspecified | H | Define <0.6 or "two plausible explanations" as low-confidence. |

---

### Questions (blocking progress)

1. **BH or 2σ — which primary filter?** The permutation-BH approach is methodologically cleaner but requires implementation of a permutation loop. The 2σ-only approach is simpler and defensible at this corpus size. This is a design choice with cost tradeoffs — resolve before spec is handed to implementers.

2. **Does the sentinel reset on baseline refresh, or does it stay anchored to the original establishment value?** The two interpretations have opposite failure modes (false alarms vs. losing the anchor). Decide which failure mode is worse for the loop's trust model.

### Known (confirmed by code/docs)

Fix: domain habit "name the segment on every reported number when the query filters by segment."
- **Retrieval/context-selection is eval-invisible by design** (audit + DL-0022): eval injects `metric_context + schema_context`; the suite does not test disambiguation or retrieval selection.

## Q1 — Are the candidate types the right and sufficient levers? Are big levers missing?

**Type-2 (habits/notes) — AGREE.**
The worked example is the canonical proof: the failure is in the findings-generation step (L1 passes, L2a:attribution fails). A DOMAIN-scoped habit is the most surgical fix — it adds a rule to the prose layer without touching SQL logic. Correctly modeled as MEDIUM blast-radius.

**Type-1 (prompt/system-instruction edits) — AGREE with a precision gap.**
IRIS has at minimum two prompt surfaces: a SQL-generation prompt and a findings-prose prompt. An L1 failure cluster (wrong SQL) needs a SQL-prompt edit. An L2a:attribution cluster needs a findings-prose edit. The design classifies both as Type-1 and distinguishes only by scope (global prefix vs lane suffix), not by which internal IRIS prompt is the target. **OBJECT**: without specifying *which* IRIS prompt a Type-1 candidate targets, the generator may emit syntactically valid diffs that touch the wrong surface. Add a required `target_prompt` field (`sql_generation | findings_prose | system_prefix`) to Type-1 candidates.

**Type-3 (tool schema/description) — AGREE (covers a real but rare lever).**
IRIS uses tools (e.g. SQL executor, metric registry lookup). A tool description that misrepresents available columns or output format can cause downstream attribution failures. Correctly classified MEDIUM.

**Type-4 (retrieval-corpus) — AGREE on routing, OBJECT on completeness.**
Correct that eval injects context directly → retrieval changes are eval-invisible → human queue. But the design doesn't acknowledge the implication: **metric disambiguation is a large, persistent class of real IRIS failures** (wrong metric definition chosen, wrong segment definition assumed) and is entirely outside this loop's scoring reach. The generator can flag it only as a Type-4 candidate (human queue), and if that queue has no SLA, those failures compound unaddressed. The design should surface this as a **structural blind spot**: any failure the generator traces to the retrieval/disambiguation step gets a Type-4 note, but the loop has zero closed-loop leverage over it. Users expecting the loop to improve IRIS comprehensively need to know this upfront.

**Type-5 (routing/classifier code) — AGREE, but eval-invisible for non-WAREHOUSE lanes.**
The suite covers only WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS. A routing bug that misdirects a WAREHOUSE query to a different lane would never appear as a failure in the suite. Low risk in practice since the suite is monolane, but worth noting.

**Missing lever — OBJECT.**
**SQL-generation context (per-metric or per-schema instructions)** is a real IRIS lever that sits between Type-1 (prompt) and Type-4 (retrieval corpus). Concretely: some L1 failures are caused not by a bad system prompt but by bad `metric_context` or `schema_context` injected for that specific metric — e.g., a metric definition that omits that `fct_daily_user_active` uses calendar days not rolling days. That's closer to a data fix than a retrieval-corpus edit. Currently it's either Type-3 (tool schema) or Type-4 (retrieval corpus), but neither is quite right — it's a **metric-registry annotation** fix. The design should either: (a) explicitly subsume this under Type-4 with a metric-registry sub-type, or (b) add a Type-4b: `metric_context_annotation`. Without a named slot, the generator has nowhere to put these findings except as a vague Type-4 human note, losing specificity.

---

## Q2 — Is (failure-tag + domain) the right clustering unit for IRIS?

**For `L2a:attribution` — AGREE.**
Attribution failures are domain-specific by nature: the segment language ("grade band", "teacher cohort") is domain vocabulary. Clustering by `attribution + engagement` yields exactly the kind of coherent, actionable hypothesis shown in the worked example. The domain co-filter improves signal quality here.

**For `L2a:fabrication` — OBJECT.**
Fabrication failures (hallucinated numbers not derivable from executed rows) tend to cluster by **query pattern** (windowed aggregations, multi-step derived calculations, year-over-year comparisons) rather than by domain. A generator seeing `fabrication + engagement` may produce a domain habit like "double-check engagement numbers," which is unfalsifiable. The better clustering axis for fabrication is query-type: "computed-aggregation questions" vs "lookup questions." The fallback to `query-pattern-tag` (§B) handles this partially — but only as a fallback when domain+tag is below N. **Recommend**: for `fabrication` and `omission` tags specifically, invert the priority — cluster first by query-pattern-tag, use domain as the secondary co-filter.

**For `L2a:omission` / `required-fact-missing` — PARTIALLY AGREE.**
Omission failures (the response doesn't mention a required fact) are often query-type-driven (e.g., "trend questions always need a direction claim") but can also be domain-driven (engagement queries need retention context, revenue queries need churn context). Mixed — the current design's fallback handles it, but a heuristic "prefer query-pattern for fabrication/omission, prefer domain for attribution" would be more actionable than a size-only fallback trigger.

**Lane co-filter — AGREE.**
Degenerate now (all 25 pairs are WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS), but correctly forward-compatible.

---

## Q3 — Will shared prompt/habit changes help one cluster without breaking other query types?

**DOMAIN-scoped habits — AGREE on the mechanism, OBJECT on coverage assurance.**
The fix "name the segment on every reported number" as `scope: DOMAIN, scope_key: engagement` is correctly scoped. It fires only for engagement queries and doesn't touch revenue or teachers habits. The regression gate (§G) and whole-suite scoring provide the mechanical check.

However: **25 pairs, with ~4–6 pairs per domain, is thin for cross-domain regression detection.** A DOMAIN habit approved with zero regressions in the suite could still degrade production behavior in that domain on query types not represented in the 25 pairs. The design acknowledges this residual risk globally (§E "25-pair corpus holdout is weak → human gate is primary defense"), but there is no equivalent **cross-query-type risk note** for MEDIUM/domain-scoped candidates comparable to the cross-lane risk note for HIGH/prefix candidates (§G). **Recommend**: for MEDIUM tier, the confounder card (§I) should include a "within-domain coverage note" — how many distinct query types in the suite does this domain have, and which query types are unrepresented.

**GLOBAL habits and HIGH/prefix prompt edits — AGREE with caveats already in design.**
The cross-lane risk note in §G correctly surfaces the WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS-only scope of the suite. No additional issue.

**Type-1 SQL-prompt edits — AGREE with one concrete risk.**
If a generator proposes a SQL-generation prompt edit to fix an L1 failure cluster (e.g., "always filter by calendar date, not rolling"), that edit may break queries where rolling windows are correct. The suite has only 3 advanced pairs (window functions / top-N) — far too few to catch SQL-logic regressions. The regression gate will catch failures in the 25 pairs, but the coverage gap means a wrongly-targeted SQL prompt edit may pass the gate and degrade production. The cross-lane risk note in §G doesn't cover this (it's intra-lane). **Recommend**: L1-targeting Type-1 candidates (SQL prompt edits) should carry an explicit **"SQL-logic coverage note"** in the confounder card: "Only N advanced/window-function pairs exist in suite; SQL-logic changes have elevated uncovered-case risk."

---

## Q4 — Is excluding eval-fixture edits from the generator correct? Does IRIS need fixture fixes routed somewhere concrete?

**Excluding fixtures from scoring — AGREE.**
Fixture changes contaminate the optimization signal. A change that tweaks `expected_answer_facts` to accept the agent's actual output would trivially pass eval while worsening real quality. Meta-firewall is correct.

**Fixture-gap path (§H) — AGREE on mechanism, OBJECT on operationalization.**
The FIXTURE-GAP NOTE structure (`{fixture_id, failure_tag, transcript evidence agent was correct, missing/ambiguous property, proposed fixture change, confidence}`) is well-specified. The instruction to prefer a fixture-gap note over a weak-evidence prompt candidate is domain-correct: given the audit found `expected_answer_facts` are "loose and gameable" and the P0 audit is a prerequisite, early loop runs are likely to encounter a significant number of fixture gaps.

**OBJECT — the fixture-gap queue has no stated owner, SLA, or processing mechanism.**
"P0 fixture-audit queue" is mentioned but undefined. If fixture-gap notes accumulate without being processed, the generator will keep seeing the same cases as failures, the 25-pair corpus shrinks effectively (those cases are permanently ambiguous), and the loop stalls. Given the DL-0022 P0 prerequisite (expected_answer_facts audit) was not done before the generator design was written, the queue could fill immediately. **Recommend**: specify (a) who is responsible for processing fixture-gap notes (human reviewer, dedicated audit pass, or queued PR), (b) a review cadence (e.g., every 3 loop runs or before any baseline refresh), and (c) a block: if the fixture-gap queue exceeds M unreviewed notes (M=5 suggested), the loop halts emission of candidates from affected clusters — analogous to the LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE sentinel.

**OBJECT — generator's ability to distinguish "fixture wrong" from "agent wrong" is uncalibrated.**
The generator uses transcript evidence to decide whether the agent was correct or the fixture was wrong. For L2a:attribution specifically (worked example), this is tractable — the executed rows show the segment, the prose doesn't, so agent is clearly wrong. But for `L2a:omission` and `required-fact-missing` failures, the distinction is much harder: was the required fact *actually* present in the data and the agent failed to mention it, or was the fixture's `required` flag overly strict? Without the P0 fixture audit complete, the generator will make unreliable fixture-vs-agent calls. **Recommend**: until the P0 expected_answer_facts audit is complete, the generator should be instructed that any `required-fact-missing` or `omission` failure should *default* to a fixture-gap note rather than a prompt candidate, with confidence=LOW, and not count toward top-5.

---

## Recommended Acceptance Criteria

1. **Type-1 candidates carry `target_prompt` field** (`sql_generation | findings_prose | system_prefix`); a Type-1 candidate targeting `findings_prose` cannot be emitted for a cluster whose failures are all L1 (SQL); rejected at generation time.
2. **For `L2a:fabrication` and `L2a:omission` clusters**, the generator uses `query-pattern-tag` as the primary clustering axis; domain is applied as a secondary co-filter only when N≥4 within a query pattern.
3. **MEDIUM-tier candidates include a within-domain coverage note** in the confounder card: count of distinct query types represented for that domain in the 25-pair suite, and an explicit flag when fewer than 3 query types are covered.
4. **L1-targeting Type-1 candidates (SQL prompt edits) carry a "SQL-logic coverage note"** in the confounder card, noting the count of advanced/window-function pairs in suite.
5. **Fixture-gap queue has a defined owner and review cadence** (e.g., every 3 loop runs); if unreviewed fixture-gap count exceeds M=5, emission from affected clusters is blocked with a FIXTURE-GAP-BACKLOG flag, analogous to LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE.
6. **Until P0 expected_answer_facts audit is complete**, any `required-fact-missing` or `omission` failure defaults to a fixture-gap note (confidence=LOW), not a prompt candidate; this bypass condition is removable by a human flag once the audit is done.
7. **Metric-disambiguation failures (retrieval step)** are classified as Type-4 sub-type `metric_registry_annotation` and emitted as a distinct line in the morning report (count + examples), separate from retrieval-corpus edits, so the structural blind spot is visible rather than buried in the human-judgment queue.
8. **The sentinel (§K)** uses an L2a:attribution case (not L2b or L3) as its re-score target, since L2a is deterministic at temp=0 and provides a stable health signal; L2b/L3 σ would make a sentinel noisy.

---

## Open Decisions

1. **Which IRIS internal prompts exist and are agent-modifiable?** The generator needs the list (SQL-gen system prompt, findings-prose system prompt, any lane-specific suffixes) before it can produce well-formed Type-1 diffs. Currently unspecified.
2. **What is the canonical domain key list for NoteScope?** The golden set implies: `engagement, revenue, teachers, parents, dojo_islands, tutor_trials`. Is this locked? Can new domains be added mid-loop without a baseline refresh?
3. **Who owns the fixture-gap queue and on what cadence?** No owner or SLA defined; the loop can stall without this.
4. **Should `required-fact-missing` failures be generator-blocked until P0 audit completes?** The design doesn't state this; recommend yes (acceptance criterion 6 above).
5. **Does the generator see `metric_context` and `schema_context` for each case?** If yes, it can reason about metric-registry annotation fixes. If not, Type-4 notes will be underspecified and unactionable.

**Summary:** The design is substantially improved from prior rounds and the round-2 fixes are confirmed landed. However, **three blocking statistical errors remain**: the BH+2σ dual-filter is methodologically malformed, the normality assumption on the net statistic is violated at N=25, and the variance propagation formula ignores within-session cross-case judge correlation. All 11 round-2 fixes are confirmed present in sections A–K. No round-2 blocker regressed.

**A. Candidate types + blast-radius tier — OBJECT (one gap)**

The CROSS-LANE RISK NOTE is required for "HIGH/prefix (Type-1) candidates" only (section G). But HIGH/global Type-2 candidates (global reflections) also fire across every domain and lane of the agent. A global note like "always name the segment on every reported number" is as cross-lane as a prefix edit, and the suite only covers WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS. The risk note obligation is absent for this case.

*Fix:* In section G, change "For HIGH/prefix (Type-1) candidates" → "For all HIGH-tier candidates (Type-1 global prefix **and** Type-2 global scope)."

**B. Input unit (failure cluster) — OBJECT (one unspecified constant)**

Co-filter by `(L2a failure-tag + domain + lane)` with L2b as advisory and L3 excluded until κ≥0.7 is correct and aligns with DL-0022. The fallback clustering axis is sound. **But** section B says "fallback clustering axis = query-pattern-tag when a tag+domain cluster is < N" and N is never defined. This is a different N than the min-cluster-size N=4 in section C. An implementer will invent it.

*Fix:* Add `[fallback-cluster-N tunable, seed: 3]` alongside the other tunable constants.

---

**C. Min cluster size — AGREE with advisory**

N≥4 / 50/50 / CANNOT-VALIDATE tagging is correct. The design correctly acknowledges the residual ("holdout is weak"). **Advisory only:** At N=4, holdout N=2. For a cluster consisting entirely of failing cases, if the LLM has ~10% natural variability near the pass/fail boundary, P(≥1 of 2 holdout cases flip to pass by chance) ≈ 19%. The confounder card already includes holdout N, but the human reviewer may not realize what that N implies about false-pass probability.

*Recommendation (not blocking):* Add to the confounder card a literal note: "Holdout N=2 → ~15–20% false-pass rate from judge variability alone. Human judgment is the primary defense." This is honest to the acknowledged residual.

Odd-N rounding (N=5 → 2 train/3 holdout or vice versa) is unspecified but low-stakes; default to ceiling for holdout is fine. Mark it.

---

**D. Generation — OBJECT (one operationalization gap)**

K≤3 and cross-cluster dedup before ranking are both sound. **But** section D specifies dedup by "cosine >0.9 [tunable]" on "(type+diff)" without naming the embedding model. For prose diffs ("add a sentence about segments") vs code diffs (a schema field rename), two very different models produce very different similarity spaces. A general-purpose embedding might merge "always name the segment" and "always name the time window" (both surface-similar) when they target distinct failure modes, causing genuine candidates to be incorrectly merged.

*Fix:* Specify embedding surface: embed `"{type}|{scope}|{scope_key}|{first 400 chars of diff}"` using the same model family as the generator (consistency). Add: "if type differs (e.g. Type-1 vs Type-2), skip cosine check — never merge across types regardless of diff similarity."

Section J: baseline refreshes on model bump OR 5 approved candidates landed. If refresh occurs at run N+3, a case quarantined at N-1 still has 5 runs left on its clock. After the refresh the baseline resets, but the quarantine doesn't. Result: a case that influenced pre-refresh generator outputs can enter training immediately post-refresh, leaking information across the refresh boundary.

*Fix:* Add to section E: "Baseline refresh resets all quarantine clocks. Cases held out in the run immediately preceding the refresh are re-quarantined for `[N+7]` runs from the refresh date."

**F. Scoring / ranking — OBJECT (three blocking statistical issues)**

**F1 — BH after 2σ pre-filter is methodologically malformed (blocking):**

Applying Benjamini-Hochberg *after* a 2σ pre-filter is not how multiple-comparisons correction works. BH must be applied to the **full** set of M candidate hypotheses simultaneously. The 2σ pre-filter rejects H₀ for any candidate with z<2 — it has already performed M individual tests at α≈0.023. Applying BH to the surviving subset inflates the effective FDR because the denominator (total hypotheses tested) is artificially small: BH controls FDR at `(k/m)×q` where m is the full hypothesis count, but you've replaced m with m'<m. Counterintuitively, this also isn't uniformly conservative — it can accept candidates that BH on the full set would have rejected if those candidates happen to land in a high rank among survivors.

*Fix:* Choose exactly one of:
- **(a) Permutation BH only (recommended):** For each candidate, compute a permutation p-value (reshuffle which cases the candidate improves vs baseline, compute net, repeat 1000×, p = fraction ≥ observed net). Apply BH at q=0.05 across ALL M candidates. Drop the 2σ pre-filter — BH subsumes it.
- **(b) 2σ threshold only:** Keep the 2σ threshold as the sole filter. Drop BH — it is redundant if σ is well-estimated; the per-test α≈0.023 already controls per-comparison error, and at M≤30 candidates the Bonferroni correction would be 0.023/30≈0.001, which is more conservative than BH anyway. Explicitly acknowledge this as the design choice.

Do not use both in series.

**F2 — 2σ assumes normality; net is discrete and non-normal at N=25 (blocking):**

`net = Σ(moved-to-pass × severity) − Σ(regressions × severity)` is a weighted sum of at most 25 binary outcomes with weights ∈ {1,2,3}. This is a discrete distribution. The CLT does not apply at N=25 with a handful of active cases per cluster. In practice, net takes values like {-6, -5, …, 0, …, +9} with probabilities concentrated near zero. The 2σ threshold assumes net/(σ(net)) ~ N(0,1) under H₀, which is incorrect for small discrete sums — it will over-reject (too permissive) in the tails and under-reject near center.

*Fix:* Either switch to permutation p-values (which makes F1 and F2 the same fix), or explicitly add: "The 2σ threshold is a heuristic approximation; for any candidate where net ≤ 3 (i.e., a single L1 win), the normal approximation is unreliable — flag for human review regardless of σ calculation."

**F3 — Var(net) formula assumes across-case independence; within-session judge correlation is real (significant):**

`Var(net) = 9·Var(L1) + 4·Var(L2a) + 1·Var(L2b)` assumes zero covariance across the 25 cases. In practice, a single LLM judge scoring all 25 pairs in one session exhibits within-session correlation: anchoring on early judgments, position bias, and session-level "mood" effects (Zheng et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024). If within-session covariance is positive — scores trend high or low together — the true Var(net) exceeds the formula's estimate, making the 2σ threshold *too permissive* (candidates clear it more easily than they should).

The 5-held-aside-twice procedure (at temp=0) measures *within-case* variance (does the same response score differently on re-runs?) but not *across-case* covariance (do all responses in a session trend together?).

*Fix:* Add a cross-case covariance probe to the σ re-estimation procedure: score the same 5 held-aside responses in two orderings (forward and reverse); if the mean net changes by more than 0.5 severity-weighted points between orderings, apply a 1.5× multiplier to σ(net) for that run to conservatively account for the ordering effect. Alternatively, if using permutation p-values (the F1 fix), this concern is subsumed — permutations are computed from the fixed scoring order, so any order effect is captured in the empirical null.

*Fix:* Specify: "CANNOT-VALIDATE candidates appear in a separate section of the report, below the top-5 validated ranking. They do not count against the 5-slot cap. A separate human-judgment queue section lists them in cluster order, with the CANNOT-VALIDATE flag prominently marked."

The refresh trigger, cumulative drift guard, and delta-vs-last-baseline comparison are all sound. **Advisory:** When the CUMULATIVE-REGRESSION flag fires (newly-failing cases at refresh), the spec cannot attribute regression to a specific landed candidate — only to the set of ≤5 candidates that landed since the prior refresh. After a baseline refresh, the sentinel's net legitimately changes — if the baseline improves (some target cases now pass), the sentinel's net contribution drops to zero. *Fix:* "After each baseline refresh, re-score the sentinel and update its expected net to the new score. LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE triggers only if the sentinel's net in run N is **below its net at the immediately prior run** (delta < 0 run-over-run), not vs the original establishment value. - **Retrieval/context-selection is eval-invisible by design** (audit + DL-0022): eval injects `metric_context + schema_context`; the suite does not test disambiguation or retrieval selection.
- **`expected_answer_facts` are loose and gameable** (audit §1): mention-checkable, no negative tests, no required-numeric audit yet — P0 prerequisite not yet done.
- **Two prompt surfaces exist in IRIS**: a SQL-generation prompt and a findings/prose-generation prompt. Only the output of both combined is graded.
- **NoteScope taxonomy for IRIS exists** (habits/notes system supports GLOBAL / DOMAIN / TABLE / USER scopes) but the canonical domain key list (engagement, revenue, teachers, parents, dojo_islands, tutor-trials) is sourced from the golden set, not formally locked.

## Q1 — Are the candidate types the right and sufficient levers? Are big levers missing?

**Type-2 (habits/notes) — AGREE.**
The worked example is the canonical proof: the failure is in the findings-generation step (L1 passes, L2a:attribution fails). A DOMAIN-scoped habit is the most surgical fix — it adds a rule to the prose layer without touching SQL logic. Correctly modeled as MEDIUM blast-radius.

**Type-1 (prompt/system-instruction edits) — AGREE with a precision gap.**
IRIS has at minimum two prompt surfaces: a SQL-generation prompt and a findings-prose prompt. An L1 failure cluster (wrong SQL) needs a SQL-prompt edit. An L2a:attribution cluster needs a findings-prose edit. The design classifies both as Type-1 and distinguishes only by scope (global prefix vs lane suffix), not by which internal IRIS prompt is the target. **OBJECT**: without specifying *which* IRIS prompt a Type-1 candidate targets, the generator may emit syntactically valid diffs that touch the wrong surface. Add a required `target_prompt` field (`sql_generation | findings_prose | system_prefix`) to Type-1 candidates.

**Type-3 (tool schema/description) — AGREE (covers a real but rare lever).**
IRIS uses tools (e.g. SQL executor, metric registry lookup). A tool description that misrepresents available columns or output format can cause downstream attribution failures. Correctly classified MEDIUM.

**Type-4 (retrieval-corpus) — AGREE on routing, OBJECT on completeness.**
Correct that eval injects context directly → retrieval changes are eval-invisible → human queue. But the design doesn't acknowledge the implication: **metric disambiguation is a large, persistent class of real IRIS failures** (wrong metric definition chosen, wrong segment definition assumed) and is entirely outside this loop's scoring reach. The generator can flag it only as a Type-4 candidate (human queue), and if that queue has no SLA, those failures compound unaddressed. The design should surface this as a **structural blind spot**: any failure the generator traces to the retrieval/disambiguation step gets a Type-4 note, but the loop has zero closed-loop leverage over it. Users expecting the loop to improve IRIS comprehensively need to know this upfront.

**Type-5 (routing/classifier code) — AGREE, but eval-invisible for non-WAREHOUSE lanes.**
The suite covers only WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS. A routing bug that misdirects a WAREHOUSE query to a different lane would never appear as a failure in the suite. The cross-lane risk note in §G is the right mitigation for HIGH candidates, but routing bugs specifically won't generate candidates at all — they produce silent mis-routes. Low risk in practice since the suite is monolane, but worth noting.

**Missing lever — OBJECT.**
**SQL-generation context (per-metric or per-schema instructions)** is a real IRIS lever that sits between Type-1 (prompt) and Type-4 (retrieval corpus). Concretely: some L1 failures are caused not by a bad system prompt but by bad `metric_context` or `schema_context` injected for that specific metric — e.g., a metric definition that omits that `fct_daily_user_active` uses calendar days not rolling days. That's closer to a data fix than a retrieval-corpus edit. Currently it's either Type-3 (tool schema) or Type-4 (retrieval corpus), but neither is quite right — it's a **metric-registry annotation** fix. The design should either: (a) explicitly subsume this under Type-4 with a metric-registry sub-type, or (b) add a Type-4b: `metric_context_annotation`. Without a named slot, the generator has nowhere to put these findings except as a vague Type-4 human note, losing specificity.

---

## Q2 — Is (failure-tag + domain) the right clustering unit for IRIS?

**For `L2a:attribution` — AGREE.**
Attribution failures are domain-specific by nature: the segment language ("grade band", "teacher cohort") is domain vocabulary. Clustering by `attribution + engagement` yields exactly the kind of coherent, actionable hypothesis shown in the worked example. The domain co-filter improves signal quality here.

**For `L2a:fabrication` — OBJECT.**
Fabrication failures (hallucinated numbers not derivable from executed rows) tend to cluster by **query pattern** (windowed aggregations, multi-step derived calculations, year-over-year comparisons) rather than by domain. A generator seeing `fabrication + engagement` may produce a domain habit like "double-check engagement numbers," which is unfalsifiable. The better clustering axis for fabrication is query-type: "computed-aggregation questions" vs "lookup questions." The fallback to `query-pattern-tag` (§B) handles this partially — but only as a fallback when domain+tag is below N. **Recommend**: for `fabrication` and `omission` tags specifically, invert the priority — cluster first by query-pattern-tag, use domain as the secondary co-filter.

**For `L2a:omission` / `required-fact-missing` — PARTIALLY AGREE.**
Omission failures (the response doesn't mention a required fact) are often query-type-driven (e.g., "trend questions always need a direction claim") but can also be domain-driven (engagement queries need retention context, revenue queries need churn context). Mixed — the current design's fallback handles it, but a heuristic "prefer query-pattern for fabrication/omission, prefer domain for attribution" would be more actionable than a size-only fallback trigger.

**Lane co-filter — AGREE.**
Degenerate now (all 25 pairs are WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS), but correctly forward-compatible.

---

## Q3 — Will shared prompt/habit changes help one cluster without breaking other query types?

**DOMAIN-scoped habits — AGREE on the mechanism, OBJECT on coverage assurance.**
The fix "name the segment on every reported number" as `scope: DOMAIN, scope_key: engagement` is correctly scoped. It fires only for engagement queries and doesn't touch revenue or teachers habits. The regression gate (§G) and whole-suite scoring provide the mechanical check.

However: **25 pairs, with ~4–6 pairs per domain, is thin for cross-domain regression detection.** A DOMAIN habit approved with zero regressions in the suite could still degrade production behavior in that domain on query types not represented in the 25 pairs. The design acknowledges this residual risk globally (§E "25-pair corpus holdout is weak → human gate is primary defense"), but there is no equivalent **cross-query-type risk note** for MEDIUM/domain-scoped candidates comparable to the cross-lane risk note for HIGH/prefix candidates (§G). **Recommend**: for MEDIUM tier, the confounder card (§I) should include a "within-domain coverage note" — how many distinct query types in the suite does this domain have, and which query types are unrepresented.

**GLOBAL habits and HIGH/prefix prompt edits — AGREE with caveats already in design.**
The cross-lane risk note in §G correctly surfaces the WAREHOUSE_ANALYSIS-only scope of the suite. No additional issue.

**Type-1 SQL-prompt edits — AGREE with one concrete risk.**
If a generator proposes a SQL-generation prompt edit to fix an L1 failure cluster (e.g., "always filter by calendar date, not rolling"), that edit may break queries where rolling windows are correct. The suite has only 3 advanced pairs (window functions / top-N) — far too few to catch SQL-logic regressions. The regression gate will catch failures in the 25 pairs, but the coverage gap means a wrongly-targeted SQL prompt edit may pass the gate and degrade production. The cross-lane risk note in §G doesn't cover this (it's intra-lane). **Recommend**: L1-targeting Type-1 candidates (SQL prompt edits) should carry an explicit **"SQL-logic coverage note"** in the confounder card: "Only N advanced/window-function pairs exist in suite; SQL-logic changes have elevated uncovered-case risk."

---

## Q4 — Is excluding eval-fixture edits from the generator correct? Does IRIS need fixture fixes routed somewhere concrete?

**Excluding fixtures from scoring — AGREE.**
Fixture changes contaminate the optimization signal. A change that tweaks `expected_answer_facts` to accept the agent's actual output would trivially pass eval while worsening real quality. Meta-firewall is correct.

**Fixture-gap path (§H) — AGREE on mechanism, OBJECT on operationalization.**
The FIXTURE-GAP NOTE structure (`{fixture_id, failure_tag, transcript evidence agent was correct, missing/ambiguous property, proposed fixture change, confidence}`) is well-specified. The instruction to prefer a fixture-gap note over a weak-evidence prompt candidate is domain-correct: given the audit found `expected_answer_facts` are "loose and gameable" and the P0 audit is a prerequisite, early loop runs are likely to encounter a significant number of fixture gaps.

**OBJECT — the fixture-gap queue has no stated owner, SLA, or processing mechanism.**
"P0 fixture-audit queue" is mentioned but undefined. If fixture-gap notes accumulate without being processed, the generator will keep seeing the same cases as failures, the 25-pair corpus shrinks effectively (those cases are permanently ambiguous), and the loop stalls. Given the DL-0022 P0 prerequisite (expected_answer_facts audit) was not done before the generator design was written, the queue could fill immediately. **Recommend**: specify (a) who is responsible for processing fixture-gap notes (human reviewer, dedicated audit pass, or queued PR), (b) a review cadence (e.g., every 3 loop runs or before any baseline refresh), and (c) a block: if the fixture-gap queue exceeds M unreviewed notes (M=5 suggested), the loop halts emission of candidates from affected clusters — analogous to the LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE sentinel.

**OBJECT — generator's ability to distinguish "fixture wrong" from "agent wrong" is uncalibrated.**
The generator uses transcript evidence to decide whether the agent was correct or the fixture was wrong. For L2a:attribution specifically (worked example), this is tractable — the executed rows show the segment, the prose doesn't, so agent is clearly wrong. But for `L2a:omission` and `required-fact-missing` failures, the distinction is much harder: was the required fact *actually* present in the data and the agent failed to mention it, or was the fixture's `required` flag overly strict? Without the P0 fixture audit complete, the generator will make unreliable fixture-vs-agent calls. **Recommend**: until the P0 expected_answer_facts audit is complete, the generator should be instructed that any `required-fact-missing` or `omission` failure should *default* to a fixture-gap note rather than a prompt candidate, with confidence=LOW, and not count toward top-5.

---

## Recommended Acceptance Criteria

1. **Type-1 candidates carry `target_prompt` field** (`sql_generation | findings_prose | system_prefix`); a Type-1 candidate targeting `findings_prose` cannot be emitted for a cluster whose failures are all L1 (SQL); rejected at generation time.
2. **For `L2a:fabrication` and `L2a:omission` clusters**, the generator uses `query-pattern-tag` as the primary clustering axis; domain is applied as a secondary co-filter only when N≥4 within a query pattern.
3. **MEDIUM-tier candidates include a within-domain coverage note** in the confounder card: count of distinct query types represented for that domain in the 25-pair suite, and an explicit flag when fewer than 3 query types are covered.
4. **L1-targeting Type-1 candidates (SQL prompt edits) carry a "SQL-logic coverage note"** in the confounder card, noting the count of advanced/window-function pairs in suite.
5. **Fixture-gap queue has a defined owner and review cadence** (e.g., every 3 loop runs); if unreviewed fixture-gap count exceeds M=5, emission from affected clusters is blocked with a FIXTURE-GAP-BACKLOG flag, analogous to LOOP-HEALTH-FAILURE.
6. **Until P0 expected_answer_facts audit is complete**, any `required-fact-missing` or `omission` failure defaults to a fixture-gap note (confidence=LOW), not a prompt candidate; this bypass condition is removable by a human flag once the audit is done.
7. **Metric-disambiguation failures (retrieval step)** are classified as Type-4 sub-type `metric_registry_annotation` and emitted as a distinct line in the morning report (count + examples), separate from retrieval-corpus edits, so the structural blind spot is visible rather than buried in the human-judgment queue.
8. **The sentinel (§K)** uses an L2a:attribution case (not L2b or L3) as its re-score target, since L2a is deterministic at temp=0 and provides a stable health signal; L2b/L3 σ would make a sentinel noisy.

---

## Open Decisions

1. **Which IRIS internal prompts exist and are agent-modifiable?** The generator needs the list (SQL-gen system prompt, findings-prose system prompt, any lane-specific suffixes) before it can produce well-formed Type-1 diffs. Currently unspecified.
2. **What is the canonical domain key list for NoteScope?** The golden set implies: `engagement, revenue, teachers, parents, dojo_islands, tutor_trials`. Is this locked? Can new domains be added mid-loop without a baseline refresh?
3. **Who owns the fixture-gap queue and on what cadence?** No owner or SLA defined; the loop can stall without this.
4. **Should `required-fact-missing` failures be generator-blocked until P0 audit completes?** The design doesn't state this; recommend yes (acceptance criterion 6 above).
5. **Does the generator see `metric_context` and `schema_context` for each case?** If yes, it can reason about metric-registry annotation fixes. If not, Type-4 notes will be underspecified and unactionable.
